newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain recovery on track after production data.
newsitem.headline: Spain recovery on track after production data.

text.p: A 17.7-percent surge in Spanish April industrial production after March's 0.2-percent fall on Thursday offered analysts the best proof yet that Spain's recovery is well on track.
Spain, which has one of the highest growth rates in Europe and record low inflation, is in prime position to increase state receipts and meet budget deficit goals.
But the same outlook is also suggesting an 18-month-old monetary easing cycle is reaching an end.

"I was expecting high growth in industrial production, but not this high. I forecast 8.5 percent, and it came out 17.7 percent," said Riccardo Barbieri, economist at Morgan Stanley. "Such a high rise is not possible without a strong recovery."
Earlier on Thursday, the national statistic institute INE also said the less volatile calendar-adjusted figure rose 12.5 percent from a year ago and 4.0 percent in March.

"Unlike the rest of Europe, (Spanish) domestic demand is picking up," said Gwyn Hacche at HSBC in London. "The pace of the recovery in Spain is strong. April figures can overstate the trend...but we have a strong recovery, which reflects strong exports, and the new feature seems to be the pick-up in consumption."
Spain's Economy Ministry said in its latest monthly report on Thursday that private consumption showed a strong recovery during the first months of the year.
After first-quarter gross domestic product rose 2.9 percent year-on-year, official estimates of three-percent 1997 growth are not seen as too optimistic.
Instead, analysts are starting to look at the risks of higher growth, which will likely outpace that of other European countries.
The Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development recently forecast Germany to grow 2.2 percent grow this year, France 2.5 percent and Italy 1.0 percent.
Spain's strong growth suggests to some that monetary easing may no longer be needed.
"The only doubt now is that if the economy does keep going at this pace, the Bank of Spain won't cut interest rate again," said Hacche. "The wise thing seems to be to leave the rate where it is".
But analysts here said the central bank still has scope for cuts, which it could use as soon as next week.

"The (production) data are much stronger than I was expecting. But I do not think this should affect next week's decision of the Bank of Spain when it could adjust its official rate to five percent," said Valentin Fernandez, economist at Credit Lyonnais in Madrid.
Spain's key money market rate stands at 5.25 percent after being cut four consecutive times so far this year.
The next official repurchase rate agreement result is scheduled for June 24.
Given May CPI at 1.5 percent set a thirty-year record low some expect it to go ahead with another cut.

"This (production) data, despite its volatility, is a clear signal the economy is picking up...But despite it...I think there is more than 50-percent probability for a cut," said Henrik Lumholdt, economist at Bank of America in Madrid.
